data.title: A. Námerová: Steppe pyramids – the Scythian kurgans of Ukraine
data.excerpt: The title of this piece is borrowed from a 2007 exhibition in Kraków that presented the excavation of the Scythian kurgan of Velyka Ryzhanivka in Ukraine. The article follows the Scythians from their arrival in the northern Black Sea steppes in the 8th century BC to the Late Scythian culture of Crimea, and explains the terms that go with them – the Scythian triad, the animal style and the kurgan itself.
data.metaTitle: A. Námerová: Steppe pyramids – Scythian kurgans
data.metaDescription: The Scythian kurgan of Velyka Ryzhanivka in Ukraine: the “steppe pyramids” and the results of their excavation, shown at a Kraków exhibition in 2007.

children.text: The title of this piece is borrowed, and partly altered, from the name of an exhibition held in Kraków back in 2007. It was then that the wider public was shown the results of the excavation of the Scythian kurgan* of Velyka Ryzhanivka, which lies in Ukraine. Monuments of Scythian culture are not found exclusively in Ukraine, yet it is the territory in which they are dominant. Let us therefore immerse ourselves for a while in the earlier history of this region – in the times when the nomads whom ancient authors called the Scythians roamed this territory.

In the area of present-day Ukraine, in the northern Black Sea region and in more distant territories as well, many kurgans of the Scythian epoch rise above the landscape. They were discovered and investigated gradually, first by amateurs and later by archaeologists. In the nineteenth century, alongside other important archaeological discoveries, the “hunt for the treasures of the Scythians” began in what was then Russia. The mound graves often belonged to the aristocratic class and their burials contained objects of precious metals – gold, silver, electrum. It goes without saying that not every amateur discoverer of this or that mound was honest enough to bring the precious objects he had found to a museum or to the city administrator of the day. It is probably in this way that we lost a certain proportion of the finds that might have helped towards a better understanding of the culture of the Scythians. Already in antiquity the clearly visible mounds attracted various robbers and became the target of their plundering. On many of them, however, burials continued to be made right up to the medieval period. For fear of desecration, profit-seeking thieves therefore lost their appetite for a time for secretly entering their interiors. A large part of the discovered precious-metal objects attributed to the Scythian period became world-famous, above all thanks to their outstanding artistic workmanship. Many of the precious objects from the kurgans can be admired with one’s own eyes in the Hermitage in St Petersburg, Russia. Some of the originals have also been exhibited in recent decades in various European capitals.

In my studies, and in meetings with the lay public or with close friends, I have for years come up against the question that everyone will put to you first in connection with the Scythians. “Who were these Scythians?” Even scholars themselves have trouble condensing the information about them into a short characterisation. Various aspects connected with them have been and still are addressed by archaeologists, historians, linguists, in part ethnologists, more remotely art historians and related scientific disciplines. A fairly long history is bound up with them, as well as a great deal of material culture and written evidence. Occasionally one may also come across the term Scythology, literally “the science of the Scythians”. If we were nevertheless to try to find a few key words that best capture the Scythians, we would offer three most important phrases – the northern Black Sea region, nomads with no permanent roof over their heads, and the Scythian triad. We shall come to the explanation of the individual unfamiliar terms in the following sections.

children.text: Geographical position

The first surviving and complete description of the territory of the Scythians comes to us from antiquity, from the historian Herodotus (IV. 101). Before him it was Hecataeus of Miletus. Of his work, however, only fragments have survived. Herodotus described Scythia as a square, each side of which equals twenty days’ march and is four thousand stades long (roughly 700 km today). Many rivers flowed through their territory; of these, the ones navigable from the sea were, according to Herodotus: the Istros /today’s Danube/, the Tyres /today’s Dniester/, the Hipanis /today’s Southern Bug/, the Borysthenes /today’s Dnieper/, the Pantikapes /today’s Konka and Inhulets/, the Hypakyris /today’s Kalanchak/, the Gerros /today’s Molochna, or the Konka/ and the Tanais /today’s Don/ (IV, 47). The mightiest of them was the Danube, into which other rivers also flow. In today’s geographical terms we may say that these were predominantly the steppe and forest-steppe territories of Ukraine, the so-called northern Black Sea area. From the earlier period their traces can also be detected in the Kuban and even in the Near East. In the south the territories of the Scythians reached into Crimea, in the north-east they were bounded by the river Don, and in the west, at the time of their greatest expansion, the Danube formed a natural frontier. It goes without saying that during the individual periods of Scythian history the extent of their territory changed. Their neighbours over several centuries were, for example, the Sarmatians, the Getae, the Greeks, the Tauri and later also the Romans. That, in brief, is how the extent and position of the Scythians might be summed up.
The question of origins.

Who were these nomads? Where did they reach the Black Sea region from? Did they arrive here from the east, or had they inhabited this space from time immemorial? Scholars of various schools asked such questions for a long time. The provenance of the Scythians also interested the ancient authors – again Herodotus. The question of their origin thus became, for a long time, one of the most discussed topics. Where there are many questions and few answers, various interpretations arise. Two main views on this subject took shape. These are the so-called autochthonous and allochthonous theories.

Supporters of the autochthonous thesis pointed to the similarity between the material culture of the Scythians and that of the bearers of the so-called Srubnaya (Timber-Grave) culture*, which was present in the Black Sea region. In the Final Bronze Age these people inhabited a broad space between the Dniester and today’s Minusinsk region. According to this view, as early as the 8th century BC the nomadic Scythians were living in the south of Eastern Europe together with the Cimmerians; later they drove the Cimmerians out and pursued some of them in their flight into Western Asia. Its supporters also argued that in the southern part of the former Russia the Iron Age began in the 7th century BC, while in Siberia and in the eastern part of Central Asia the Bronze Age tradition long survived. If the Scythians had come from the depths of Asia, they would have had to bring with them archaic forms and not a developed Iron Age culture. According to some scholars, the “original homeland” of the Scythians therefore lay east of the river Don, where their neighbours were initially, from the Caspian Sea, the Massagetae and the Issedones. The thesis of the autochthonous origin of the Scythians had many shortcomings and in the nineteen-seventies it became the target of criticism from specialists in Scythian culture.

The second theory may, in other words, be called the migration theory. It assumes that the “Scythians” had already been formed in the Asian region and migrated into the northern Black Sea region, arriving here as a culture with the elements characteristic of them. Until the 1970s the original homeland of the Scythians was placed only very generally in the “depths of Asia”. The defenders of this idea were also helped by Herodotus’s report of the pressure exerted on them in Asia by the nomadic Massagetae (Herodotus, IV. 11). Supporters of this thesis were greatly assisted by the discoveries of the large royal kurgans in Tuva – Arzhan 1, Arzhan 2 and other complexes. The Scythian triad was represented in both. The burial ritual fully agrees with the ritual of the royal Scythians from the Black Sea region. Similar manifestations and finds are known from a vast steppe territory: from the Altai, Kazakhstan, the Azov, Caucasus and Pamir regions, from the upper Ob, the Minusinsk Basin, Transbaikalia and the Ordos. According to M. P. Gryaznov, the scholar who uncovered the Arzhan 1 kurgan, this kurgan was contemporary with the pre-Scythian period in the northern Black Sea region and in Tuva it represents the earliest horizon of Scythian culture.

The two main theses presented here briefly, and above all the second of them, which is coming more and more to the fore, still contain a great many points for discussion even today. The question and the uncertainties remain open as to which archaeological culture the Scythians can be linked with genetically: whether they were the bearers of the Catacomb culture, the descendants or the direct bearers of the Srubnaya culture, or whether their whole culture should be derived from Central Asia. Today the prevailing view is that the Scythians reached the region of the northern Black Sea and the Caucasus, where their presence can be documented from roughly the 8th century BC, from the area of Asia.
History in a nutshell?

Brief, unfortunately, is not a word that can be used of it. Nevertheless, we shall attempt a short survey of the most important and most compelling events of their history, following one another chronologically. It may be said that the history begins in the 8th century BC, when elements of Scythian culture appear for the first time in the Dnieper region and in the forest-steppe. As we have already written, it is assumed that the Scythians came to the Black Sea steppes from Asia with an already developed culture, at the latest in the 7th century BC.
“An adventurous expedition to Western Asia and Egypt”

Before they consolidated their dominance over the northern Black Sea region, over the extensive steppe and forest-steppe territories, we must mention their part in the history of Western Asia. On the Black Sea coast, at the end of the 8th century BC, there was a clash between the Cimmerians, already mentioned in passing, and the Scythians. The Cimmerians, their predecessors in that territory, were pushed out of the Black Sea steppes by the Scythians, with the result that some of them turned towards Western Asia. Part of the Scythians set off in pursuit of them. The event is again mentioned by the writer Herodotus (IV. 11). During this ancient “chase” the Cimmerians invaded the kingdom of Urartu, in the reign of Rusa I (734–714 BC). We shall omit their further military actions and movements in the region. They lasted roughly until the 7th century BC. The first Scythian raids on the territories of the Near East came only a century later, in the reign of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (680–669 BC). Scholars have also found records of certain events connected with them in cuneiform tablets. In the years 675–672 BC, according to several sources, the marriage of the Scythian king Partatua (also given as Bartatua) to a daughter of king Esarhaddon took place. From 650 BC onwards we are able to detect their traces in Western Asia by means of archaeology as well. Finds of the so-called Scythian type have been made, for example, in the complexes of Norşuntepe, Karmir-Blur, Ziwiye and others. The successful campaigns of the Scythians also included the threatening of Egypt in the years 630–625 BC. The pharaoh Psamtik I (663–610 BC) came out to meet them with gifts and entreaties and persuaded them not to go any further. After their successful “sweep” against Egypt they turned back and, during the reign of Rusa II (625–585 BC), destroyed the kingdom of Urartu. The end of Scythian domination in Western Asia was brought about by the Median king Cyaxares in 594 BC. He achieved his victory not in open battle but by a ruse. He invited the leading commanders to a feast, got them drunk, slaughtered them and drove the rest out of the country. Thus ended more than twenty-eight years of Scythian domination in the Orient.
The Persian retaliation

After their defeat in Western Asia, part of the Scythians returned to the region of the northern Black Sea. A smaller group remained until the 6th century BC in the Kuban and the northern Caucasus. Their presence there at that time can also be documented by archaeological material from kurgans such as Kelermes, Kostromskaya and others. It is an open question why the traces of the Scythians in this region disappear in the 5th century. Meanwhile the remaining part of the Scythians in the region of the northern Black Sea consolidated their dominance over the territory. More and more often they came into contact with the Greek cities founded during the Great Greek colonisation. The tribe of the Tauri in Crimea was also in their vicinity. In the west, in the Danube region, there were the Thracian Getae. Their relations with the surrounding communities were for the most part peaceful. It was only the march of the Persian king Darius I against the Scythians in the years 515–513/512 BC that became an important historical event. Herodotus described the Darius episode in his fourth book and depicted it in considerable detail. Despite that, some present-day scholars have raised doubts about the truth of the campaign. If we were to stay with Herodotus’s assertion that the campaign really took place, it ended victoriously for the Scythians. In the ancient world they earned for a time the reputation of an invincible people. This event was followed by several further smaller movements of the Scythians towards the west, to the tribe of the Odrysians. Sometime in the years 480–470 BC king Ariapithes even concluded a marriage with a daughter of the king of the Odrysians. During the following centuries it was mostly a matter only of smaller quarrels of a regional character. In the 5th–4th centuries BC Scythia also reached its greatest and never-repeated flowering. Trade relations developed between them and the local Greeks. In this period the so-called rich royal kurgans appear, from which many well-known objects of precious metals come. The slow decline, however, was not long in coming.
The defeat of the greatest Scythian king

In 339 BC a battle took place in the vicinity of the Danube between Philip II of Macedon and the Scythian king Ateas. Just as about Darius, ancient writers from the Greek and Roman world also wrote about the battle mentioned above. This time the battle turned out to the disadvantage of the Scythians, because the Scythian king Ateas, said to be 90 years old, fell in the fighting. Scholars view the causes of the conflict in various ways. The battle had several unhappy consequences. The Scythians lost part of their territory around the Danube. The part that was at that time staying in so-called Lesser Scythia (the Dobruja region) remained cut off from the rest of their “fellow tribesmen”. After the fall of Ateas a general political destabilisation set in. From 339 BC onwards we are unable to document any certain king attested by sources, whether literary or archaeological. Only in the last quarter of the 4th century BC did the ancient author Diodorus Siculus (XX. 24) record a ruler by the name of Agarus. The years of his reign and the territory he administered, however, we are unable to document precisely. What is certain is that it is he who closes the so-called dynasty of the royal Scythians.
Are the Scythians still Scythians, or the Late Scythian culture in Crimea

From the 3rd century BC the so-called Late Scythian culture began to take shape. The Scythians gradually went over to a settled way of life, which was connected with the founding of settlements and towns. The whole new grouping, however, is marked by strong ethnic intermixing. The majority of the Scythians moved into the territory in the valley of the river Dnieper and into Crimea, and a small part remained in the already mentioned Dobruja. In Lesser Scythia (the Dobruja) we can record the last “breath” of the Scythians around the 1st century BC. In Crimea the Late Scythian culture survived, according to some scholars, as late as the 3rd century AD. There are various views on the causes of its emergence. Again we may speak of two main theories. The older view sees in the Late Scythian culture a genetic link to the preceding culture of the royal Scythians. In this connection we then meet with various explanations of why they adopted a settled way of life and why so-called Great Scythia ceased to exist. Many of these theories reckon with pressure from the Sarmatians, the Iranian tribes closely related to them. The increase of their material culture in the former territory of the Scythians points to this. A certain proportion of scholars believe that there may also have been a climatic change which forced some of them to move to warmer and more fertile regions. The second view advances the idea that there is no connection between the Late Scythian culture and the culture of Great Scythia. The material culture does not contain the signs and features of classical Scythian culture. The second theory proceeds from the most recent research in the Crimean region and at present the ranks of its supporters are growing. Whichever of the two we choose, the fact remains that from the third century onwards the Scythians were losing their power and that in the course of time they were assimilated.
Written records about the Scythians

The written reports referring to the Scythians can be divided into three groups. They are tablets written in cuneiform from the Near East, the testimonies of ancient authors, and epigraphic monuments from the Greek colonies on the coast of the Black Sea. At this point attention must be drawn to the linguistic affiliation of the Scythians. They are classed within the Indo-Iranian dialect group of languages, with no literary monuments. As examples, the surviving names of Scythian rulers in the works of ancient authors are cited, and the names of Scythian officials found on decrees from the ancient Black Sea cities mentioned above. A great deal of information about the Scythians was recorded precisely by the ancient authors. They wrote a great deal indeed about the Scythians and the information from them is of varied character. They appear for the first time in ancient writing in Hesiod. A fragment comes from him in which he writes of them as the Scythians who drink mare’s milk.

Herodotus’s fourth book from his work the Histories may be considered the most important and most significant source on the Scythians. Although many other authors mentioned them after him, most of the later authors almost always drew on his information. Herodotus first gives a brief history of the Scythians, describes three different genealogical legends, states the geographical position of Scythia and the various Scythian and non-Scythian tribes; of interest, too, is the characterisation of Scythian religious rituals and their pantheon in comparison with the Greek one. Part of the fourth book is the campaign of the Persian king Darius against the Scythians in 513–512 BC. The individual testimonies of Herodotus have been subjected by many scholars to deeper analysis and comparison with reality.

What Herodotus did not record was supplemented by the well-known ancient physician Hippocrates, specifically in his work Peri aeron, hydaton, topon (On Airs, Waters and Places). He writes, for instance, that wealthy Scythian women often suffered from obesity, the men from infertility, and so on.

Among the important ancient authors who mention the “Scythians” more broadly are, for example, the Greek geographer Strabo, Diodorus Siculus, Lucian, Arrian, Pliny the Elder, Ovid and others. These authors, however, belong for the most part to the period from the 1st century BC to the 2nd century AD. They draw mostly on Herodotus or on other earlier works. Occasionally they also bring new authentic reports from the Black Sea region. After the decline of Great Scythia a new phenomenon begins to come to the fore in the literature. The Scythians fulfil the function of any nomadic tribe in the Black Sea region. In many cases we are unable to determine whether the author really means the historical Scythians or some other nomadic ethnic group.
Conclusion

A great many monographs, studies, reports, catalogues or merely short articles exist about the Scythians and the various aspects of their history, archaeology and art. The variability of the topics bears witness to the constant interest on the part of scholars of various schools. Among the greatest specialists on their problems are Russian and Ukrainian scholars. After all, the territory of the royal Scythians lay precisely in the area of the former Soviet Union. For many western and Central European scholars this subject is in its way “exotic”. The translations of original Russian books into English or German are evidence of this. If the subject has interested you, you need only visit the nearest library, where you can study the whole matter in more detail.
Explanations of the individual terms
The Scythian triad

A key role in documenting a culture with similar features in the east, and also in the later European Scythia, was played by the identification of identical elements. These are three characteristic features of the culture of the Scythians, present in the kurgans and sometimes at settlements in the northern Black Sea region, as well as far away in the steppes of Eurasia. They are horse harness, weaponry (the akinakes, the gorytos, three-bladed arrowheads and the like*) and the Scythian animal style. The term was first used and defined in the 1950s by two Russian archaeologists – A. I. Meliukova and B. N. Grakov.
The animal style

This is the artistic style that characterises the Scythians and belongs to the Scythian triad. It passed through several developmental stages. At the beginning their art reflected the sensibility of the steppe nomads in Asia, which was zoomorphic. Later, during the campaigns into Asia Minor, it was inspired by oriental motifs such as sphinxes, the tree of life, the scorpion and the like. After their arrival in the Black Sea region, Greek master craftsmen intervened in their original conceptions and enriched this style with anthropomorphic figures. The individual phases of its development can be followed on finds from the kurgans and on other monuments.
A brief characterisation of the Srubnaya culture

The Srubnaya (Timber-Grave) culture takes its name from the way the dead were buried in wooden chambers – in timber frames. The bearers of this culture were semi-nomads with horse breeding and advanced metallurgy (a large number of short swords, daggers, axes, knives and so on have been found).
A brief characterisation of the Catacomb culture

A culture of the Early Bronze Age in the region of the northern Black Sea and the Caucasus, dated to 3000–2200 BC. Since the territory over which it spread was large, various regional variants also developed within it. It received its name from its specific burial rite. Beneath a heaped-up mound, individuals were buried in catacombs. Usually the dead person lay in an extended position on the right side, and near him were grave goods in the form of weapons of various metals – small axes, arrowheads, knives, but also body ornaments (finger rings) and pottery products. Occasional finds of wagons in the graves are of interest.
Kurgan

In Russian literature it is written kurgan; the Slovak form is kurhan. It is an alternative name for a burial mound, or tumulus. In the case of the culture of the Scythians this is the designation most often used. It is a larger artificial mound of earth, sometimes in combination with stone, heaped up over an inhumation grave, or occasionally a cremation grave, or over several graves. Within a mound a central grave is usually distinguished, sometimes in a specially built chamber (often robbed), together with secondary graves, which had a different significance in the individual periods. A place where mounds occur is called a barrow cemetery.

children.text: Gorytos

This is a special quiver, divided into two parts, in which the bow and the arrows were stowed. It was worn hung from the belt. In the picture above is the gold gorytos from the central grave of the Chertomlyk kurgan, of the 4th century BC. It was made to order by Greek craftsmen.
Akinakes

(Gr. ἀκινάκης) – a short (40–60 cm) sword. It was used by the Scythians, but was also popular among other Iranian communities, such as the Saka, the Persians or the Massagetae. It reached the Black Sea region through the Scythians, but finds of them are documented in the Asian region as well. In the picture is a sword in a gold sheath from a Scythian kurgan of the 4th century BC, from the site of Velyka Bilozerka.
